questions.question: In which of the following stages of the first meiotic division do the chromosomes get attached to the spindle fibers?

explanation.text: Metaphase 1: The second stage of first meiotic division. Chromosomes get arranged as a metaphase plate in the equator of the cells - midway between the 2 centrioles → Chromosome’s centromeres get attached to microtubules of the spindle via kinetochores. Kinetochore fibers pull the chromosomes toward the poles, creating tension through the cohesin complex. The tension indicates that the sister chromatids have achieved proper biorientation.
The cell monitors the attachment of microtubules to chromosomes and possibly the tension generated by the microtubules.

questions.question: Which of the following statements on Anaphase 1 is true?

options.D: Each chromosome from the pair migrates to opposite poles of the spindle

explanation.text: Anaphase 1: The third stage of first meiotic division. Each chromosome from the pair migrates to opposite poles of the spindle. No division of centromere.

questions.question: Which of the following events occurs during telophase of meiosis?

options.C: Chromatids are pulled towards the spindle poles.

explanation.text: In telophase, chromosomes unwind and return to a less condensed chromatin state. Telophase is the concluding stage of both mitosis and meiosis, following the movement of chromatids to the spindle poles. It is essential for ensuring that each daughter cell inherits an identical chromosome set, preserving genetic continuity in cell divisions.

Key events in this phase include: Chromosome Relaxation: The chromatids start to unwind and revert to chromatin, becoming less distinct under a microscope. Nuclear Envelope Reassembly: A new nuclear membrane forms around each set of separated chromatids, resulting in two distinct nuclei. Spindle Breakdown: The spindle fibers, responsible for chromosome movement, are disassembled.
Cytokinesis Begins: While telophase focuses on nuclear changes, it often coincides with cytokinesis, where the cytoplasm splits, producing two daughter cells.
**Chromatids condense into chromosomes (Option A):** This event occurs in prophase, not telophase. During prophase, chromatin condenses to form visible chromosomes.

**Nuclear envelope disintegrates (Option B):** This event happens in prophase, where the nuclear membrane breaks down to allow spindle fibers access to the chromosomes. In telophase, the nuclear envelope re-forms.
**Chromatids are pulled towards the spindle poles (Option C):** This occurs in anaphase when the chromatids are separated and moved to opposite ends of the cell by the spindle fibers.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the stage at which the primary oocyte is arrested during oogenesis before puberty?

explanation.text: The primary oocyte arrests in Prophase of meiosis I during fetal development and remains in this stage until puberty.

PGCs → Oogonia (mitotic divisions) → Primary Oocytes (arrest in prophase I) → Primordial Follicles Before Birth: Oogonia peak at 7 million → Degeneration → Remaining oocytes enter prophase I ↓ At Birth: Oocyte maturation inhibitor (OMI) causes arrest in prophase I (diplotene stage) ↓ Puberty: Pool of growing follicles established → 15–20 follicles mature monthly Formation of antral (vesicular) follicles with fluid-filled spaces → Primary Follicle ↓ Follicular Development: Follicular cells → Cuboidal (granulosa cells) → Secrete zona pellucida Theca folliculi forms → Theca interna and externa layers around granulosa cells Antrum enlarges, forming Graafian Follicle (25 mm) ↓ Ovulation: LH surge induces completion of meiosis I Formation of secondary oocyte and polar body Secondary oocyte arrests in metaphase II ↓ Fertilization Yes: Meiosis II completed No: Oocyte degenerates 24 hours post-ovulation

questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes the role of Sertoli cells during spermatogenesis?

options.A: They induce spermatogonial stem cells to initiate spermatogenesis.
options.B: They stimulate Leydig cells to produce testosterone.
options.C: They secrete androgen-binding proteins and support germ cells.
options.D: They transform type A spermatogonia into spermatids.

explanation.text: Sertoli cells play a crucial role in spermatogenesis by secreting androgen-binding proteins supporting, protecting, and nourishing the developing germ cells.

Primordial germ cells (PGCs) arrive in the gonad of a genetic male around the end of the fifth week of development. ↓ At Birth Germ cells in sex cords (Surrounded by supporting cells-Sertoli cells) ↓ Puberty Sex cords → Seminiferous tubules PGCs → Spermatogonial stem cells Type A spermatogonia form → Undergo mitosis → Type B spermatogonia ↓ Meiosis I Type B spermatogonia → Primary spermatocytes Primary spermatocytes → Prolonged prophase I (22 days) → Completion of meiosis I → Secondary spermatocytes ↓ Meiosis II Secondary spermatocytes → Meiosis II → Haploid spermatids ↓ Cytoplasmic Bridges Successive germ cells connected by cytoplasmic bridges Spermatogonia and spermatids remain embedded in Sertoli cells ↓ Hormonal Regulation LH → Leydig cells → Testosterone → Sertoli cells → Promotes spermatogenesis FSH → Sertoli cells → Testicular fluid and androgen receptor protein synthesis ↓ Spermiogenesis Spermatids → Spermatozoa Acrosome formation Nuclear condensation Formation of neck, middle piece, and tail Cytoplasm shedding (phagocytized by Sertoli cells) ↓ Final Maturation Spermatozoa → Lumen of seminiferous tubules → Epididymis (gain full motility)

questions.question: Which of the following statements is most accurate regarding the relationship between the luteinizing hormone (LH) surge and ovulation? A) The LH surge typically begins 24 hours before ovulation. B) The LH surge stimulates the release of the second polar body from the oocyte. C) The LH surge is initiated by a rise in progesterone levels from the corpus luteum. D) The peak of the LH surge occurs approximately 10-12 hours before ovulation. E) A smaller follicle size is always associated with a higher LH peak.

explanation.text: The luteinizing hormone (LH) surge plays a crucial role in the menstrual cycle, preceding ovulation. The LH surge is essential for triggering ovulation, with its peak closely preceding the release of the egg.

The surge is triggered by a significant rise in estradiol, produced by the dominant follicle, typically larger than 15mm on ultrasound. (Statement C) While the LH surge happens about 36 hours before ovulation, the LH surge peaks 10-12 hours before ovulation, making it a useful marker for timing ovulation (Statement A) It stimulates luteinization of granulosa cells, promotes progesterone production, and prompts the oocyte to resume meiosis, leading to the release of the first polar body. (Statement B) Surges with multiple peaks are linked to smaller follicle sizes before rupture and lower LH levels on the day of ovulation. (Statement E)

questions.question: Which of the following is most accurate regarding in vitro fertilization (IVF) for women with bilateral tubal blockage?

options.A: IVF is ineffective for women with bilateral tubal blockage.
options.B: Bilateral salpingectomy is always required before IVF in cases of tubal blockage.
options.C: ICSI is used to fertilize the egg in all IVF cases, regardless of sperm quality.
options.D: Preimplantation genetic testing (PGT) is necessary for women of advanced maternal age.

explanation.text: IVF provides a solution for women with bilateral tubal blockage, a condition in which both fallopian tubes are blocked, preventing natural conception. Mechanism: IVF bypasses the fallopian tubes by directly retrieving eggs from the ovaries, fertilizing them in a lab, and transferring the embryos into the uterus.

Surgical Considerations: Women with severe tubal damage may undergo bilateral salpingectomy (removal of both fallopian tubes) to improve IVF success rates by avoiding complications from dysfunctional tubes. (Option B ruled out) Success Rates: IVF success in cases of bilateral tubal blockage depends on factors like age, overall reproductive health, and egg/embryo quality.

Despite these variables, IVF remains a highly effective treatment. (Option A ruled out) The main steps of IVF include: Controlled Ovarian Hyperstimulation: Most often done using injectable gonadotropins. After about 36 hours from a trigger shot or HCG injection, egg retrieval is performed using transvaginal ultrasound-guided aspiration. Fertilization: Retrieved eggs are placed in a special medium, and normal sperm is added for insemination.

If sperm abnormalities are present, intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) is used, where a single sperm is injected directly into the egg's cytoplasm. (Option C ruled out) Embryo Assessment: After fertilization, embryos are assessed and graded. Transfer usually occurs on Day 3 or Day 5.

Preimplantation Genetic Testing (PGT): It’s a procedure used to detect genetic mutations, chromosomal translocations, or aneuploidy (abnormal number of chromosomes). It’s especially useful in cases of advanced maternal age, recurrent IVF failures, recurrent pregnancy loss, or unexplained infertility. (Option D)

questions.question: What is the correct sequence of stem cell potency based on their ability to differentiate?

explanation.text: The correct order of arrangement of stem cells based on their potency to differentiate into different cells from (highest to lowest) is Totipotent > Pluripotent > Multipotent > Oligopotent > Unipotent

questions.question: Which stage of spermatogenesis is characterised by an independent assortment of maternal and paternal chromosomes?

explanation.text: Independent assortment is the random distribution of chromosomes It occurs at Meiosis 1 where there is division from primary spermatocyte to secondary spermatocyte. It states that genes located on different chromosomes are inherited independently of each other. In other words, the allele a parent passes on for one trait does not affect the allele passed on for another trait.

During Metaphase I of meiosis, the homologous chromosomes line up in pairs at the cell's equator. The orientation of each chromosome pair is random, meaning the maternal or paternal chromosome can go into either of the two daughter cells.This random alignment is the basis of independent assortment. Independent assortment is a key factor in genetic variation. This prevents all chromosomes from the same source ending up in the same gamete.

questions.question: What is the part of the embryo that exerts morphogenetic stimulus on its adjacent part called?

explanation.text: Any part of the embryo that exerts a morphogenetic stimulus on adjacent part is known as the organiser. In morphogenetic development, organizers can be classified into different levels depending on their roles in inducing specific developmental patterns in the embryo. First level is the organiser that induces the development of new tissues. This newly developed tissue can then induce another tissue to become secondary organisers.

Therefore, there is a sequence or chain of organiser called primary, secondary and tertiary organisers. Examples of three level of organisers: Primary Organizer: Blastopore induces differentiation of notochord. Secondary Organizer: Notochord induces the development of neural tube (that forms brain and spinal cord) Tertiary Organizer: Neural tube induces segmentation of paraxial mesoderm into somites

questions.question: During fertilisation, all of the following barriers in the ovum are penetrated by the sperm except:

explanation.text: The sperm does not penetrate the nuclear membrane of oocyte Sperm must overcome three barriers to fertilize an egg: Corona Radiata Zona Pellucida Oocyte cell membrane After the fusion of sperm and oocyte cell membranes, the nucleus of ovum is converted to the female pronucleus. The nucleus of sperm become male pronucleus.

questions.question: Which of the following is not an acrosomal enzymes?

explanation.text: Alkaline phosphatase is not an acrosomal enzyme. The three main acrosomal enzymes are: acrosin, hyaluronidase and acid phosphatase. The sperm binds to the zona pellucida through the glycoprotein ligands ZP3 and ZP2(zona proteins). The binding causes the release of the acrosomal enzymes that allow the sperm to penetrate the zona pellucida. This is called an acrosomal reaction.

questions.question: Which day during Week 1 of embryonic development matches with the given image?

explanation.text: The first week of development begins with fertilization and ends with the initial stages of implantation. The image given shows Morula formation where the zygote becomes a solid ball of 16-32 cells. Cleavage: Once the zygote has reached the two-cell stage, it undergoes a series of mitotic divisions, which become smaller with each cleavage division known as blastomeres.

DAY EVENT Day 0 Fertilization: The sperm fertilizes the egg in the fallopian tube, forming a zygote (single diploid cell) Day 1 Two cell stage Day 2 Four cell stage Day 3 Twelve cell stage Day 4 Morula Formation: The zygote becomes a solid ball of 16-32 cells.

Day 5 Blastocyst Formation: The morula continues to divide and develops a fluid-filled cavity (blastocoel), which consists of the outer trophoblast (future placenta) and the inner cell mass (future embryo). Day 6&7 Implantation begins: Blastocyst attaches to the endometrial lining of the uterus and trophoblast begins to invade the uterine wall to start implantation.

questions.question: How many cells are typically present in the morula stage?

explanation.text: Morula Early stage in embryo development that occurs around day 3 or day 4 after fertilization. Formed by cleavage of compacted blastomeres. By the time the morula forms, the embryo typically consists of 16-32 blastomeres. The cells in the morula are tightly packed, forming a compact structure that resembles a mulberry.

Even though the number of cells increases, the overall size of the morula remains the same as the zygote, because cleavage divisions occur without increasing the embryo's volume. The group of cells present in the centre of morula gives rise to the inner cell mass and embryo proper and cells at the periphery (outer cell mass) are critical in the cavitation of the morula as it transitions into a blastocyst.

questions.question: What is the function of cortical reaction in fertilization?

options.A: Facilitate the entry of additional sperm into the oocyte.
options.B: Prevent polyspermy by modifying the egg's outer membrane.
options.C: Help the sperm to penetrate the zona pellucida.
options.D: Release digestive enzymes that help break down the oocyte's nucleus.

explanation.text: Process Mechanism Purpose Acrosome Reaction The acrosome (cap-like structure on the sperm head) releases hydrolytic enzymes (e.g., hyaluronidase, acrosin). These enzymes digest the zona pellucida, allowing the sperm to penetrate and reach the oocyte’s plasma membrane. Allows sperm to penetrate the zona pellucida and fertilize the oocyte.

Cortical Reaction The fusion of the sperm with the egg membrane triggers the release of cortical granules (vesicles) into the perivitelline space. The contents of these granules alter the zona pellucida and egg membrane, preventing additional sperm from binding and penetrating. Prevents polyspermy (entry of more than one sperm), ensuring viable embryo development. Zona Reaction Occurs due to the cortical reaction.
The enzymes released modify the structure of the zona pellucida, making it impenetrable to other sperm. Prevents further sperm from binding or penetrating the oocyte, ensuring only one fertilizes it.

**Facilitate the entry of additional sperm into the oocyte (Option A):** This is exactly what the cortical reaction prevents. Multiple sperm entering would lead to polyspermy, which is fatal to the embryo.

**Help the sperm to penetrate the zona pellucida (Option C):** This is the role of the acrosome reaction, not the cortical reaction. The sperm's acrosome releases enzymes to penetrate the zona pellucida before fertilization.

**Release digestive enzymes that help break down the oocyte's nucleus (Option D):** This is not a function of the cortical reaction. Also, the oocyte's nucleus is not broken down; it fuses with the sperm nucleus to form a zygote.

questions.question: During which phase of the menstrual cycle does implantation typically occur?

explanation.text: Implantation is a process by which a fertilized egg, or blastocyst, attaches to and embeds itself into the lining of the endometrium. Implantation is the result of mutual trophoblastic and endometrial action. Timing: Begins about 2-4 days after the morula enters the uterine cavity (morula is formed 3-4 days after fertilisation).

Blastocyst Stage: The fertilized egg develops into a blastocyst, which is a structure with an inner cell mass, a trophoblast layer, and a blastocoel (fluid-filled cavity). Trophoblast Cells: The outer layer of the blastocyst, called the trophoblast, plays a key role in implantation. These cells adhere to and invade the uterine lining (endometrium).

Uterine Lining: Implantation occurs in the endometrium, which is the thickened lining of the uterus, during the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle. Process: The blastocyst attaches to the endometrial lining and begins to burrow into it. Trophoblast cells secrete enzymes that help in embedding the blastocyst and establish a connection with the maternal blood supply.
Hormonal Changes: The implantation process triggers the release of hormones, such as human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), which helps maintain the corpus luteum and prevents menstruation.

questions.question: Which substance helps in the attachment of the blastocyst to the uterus?

explanation.text: Blastocyst: About the time the morula enters the uterine cavity, fluid begins to penetrate through the zona pellucida into the intercellular spaces of the inner cell mass and finally, a single cavity blastocoele formed with blastocyst. Occurs approximately 5 days after fertilization. Inner cell mass/Embryoblast: This will develop into the embryo and the associated extra-embryonic tissues.

Outer cell mass/Trophoblast: Forms part of the placenta and facilitate implantation into the uterine wall. Blastocoel: A fluid-filled cavity within the blastocyst that helps the embryo to expand and implant. L-Selectin on trophoblast cells and its carbohydrate receptors on the uterine epithelium mediate the initial attachment of the blastocyst to the uterus. Implantation is the result of mutual trophoblastic and endometrial action.

The embryoblast differentiates into epiblast cells dorsally and hypoblast cells ventrally. Some of the hypoblast are specified to form the anterior visceral endoderm (AVE) and become the cranial end of the embryo.

questions.question: What is the most characteristic event of the 3rd week of development?

explanation.text: Gastrulation: The most characteristic event occurring during the third week of gestation. The Process of the establishment of all three germ layers (ectoderm, endoderm, mesoderm) from one dimensional layer of epithelial cells, a blastula. Begins with formation of primitive streak on the surface of epiblast and becomes clearly visible as a narrow groove with slightly bulging regions in 15-16 day embryo.

The cephalic end of the streak is called the primitive node consisting of a slightly elevated area surrounding the small primitive pit. The migration of the cells of epiblast towards the primitive streak is called invagination. Cell migration and specification are controlled by fibroblast growth factor 8 (FGF8) which is synthesized by streak cells. FGF8 controls cell specification into the mesoderm by regulating BRACHYURY (T) expression.

After invagination of cells, some displace the hypoblast creating the embryonic endoderm while others come to lie between the epiblast, a newly created endoderm to form mesoderm. Cells remaining in the epiblast form an ectoderm. The epiblast through the process of gastrulation is the source of all the germ layers.
**Formation of blastocyst (Option A):** The blastocyst forms around the 5th day, much earlier than the 3rd week.
**Implantation (Option C):** Happens around the end of the first week or beginning of the second week.
**Formation of morula (Option D):** The morula is formed on day 3 or 4 after fertilization, before the blastocyst stage, so it’s much earlier than the 3rd week.

questions.question: What structure forms at the surface of the epiblast to initiate gastrulation?

explanation.text: Primitive streak/groove (structure-4) forms at the surface of epiblast to initiate gastrulation. Markings in image: 1 - Prechordal plate 2 - Primitive pit 3 - Primitive node 4 - Primitive streak/ groove Gastrulation: Description Gastrulation, occurring in the third week of gestation, establishes the three germ layers: ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm.

Structures and migration Formation of the primitive streak on the surface of the epiblast. (Option C) Initially vague, it becomes a distinct groove by days 15-16. The primitive node forms at the cephalic end of epiblast, slightly elevated with a small surrounding primitive pit. Epiblast cells migrate towards the primitive streak, become flask-shaped, detach, and move inward (invagination).

Regulation Fibroblast growth factor 8 (FGF8) regulates cell migration Mesoderm specification by downregulating E-cadherin and affecting BRACHYURY (T) expression. Formation of Germ Layers Invaginated cells displace the hypoblast to form the endoderm, some lie between epiblast and endoderm to form mesoderm, and remaining epiblast cells form ectoderm.

Prechordal Plate Forms between the notochord tip and oropharyngeal membrane from the first migrating cells, crucial for forebrain induction. Oropharyngeal Membrane At the cranial end, it is a region of tightly adhered ectoderm and endoderm cells that will become the oral cavity opening.

questions.question: A stillborn baby was noted to have the following findings. The above pathology is derived from which among the following structure shown in the image below?

explanation.text: The pathology shown is Oropharyngeal teratoma, arises from Primordial germ cells that fail to migrate to the gonadal ridge and Primordial germ cells (PGC) in the image corresponds to “2”. Markings in the image are: 1 - Allantois 2 - Primordial Germ cells (Option B) 3 - Yolk sac 4 - Heart Primordial Germ Cells (PGC): Origin and Migration of Primordial Germ Cells (PGC) 2nd week: PGC originate in the epiblast and migrate through the primitive streak. 3rd week: They are located among endoderm cells in the wall of the yolk sac, close to the allantois. 4th week: The PGC migrate by ameboid movement along the dorsal mesentery of the hindgut. 5th week: They arrive at the primitive gonads. 6th week: Invade the genital ridges.

Gonads Shortly before and during the arrival of primordial germ cells, the epithelium of the genital ridge starts to proliferate. Epithelial cells penetrate the underlying mesenchyme, forming primitive sex cords, which are irregularly shaped. In both male and female embryos, the primitive sex cords are connected to the surface epithelium.

At this stage, the gonad is called the indifferent gonad, as there is no distinction between male and female gonads yet. Pathologies associated: due to failure of migration of PGC Teratoma (oropharyngeal/sacrococcygeal) Non development of gonads
